The Brahmin and the Three Tricksters: Why Three Voices Are Not Necessarily Three Independent Pieces of Evidence
A Brahmin received a sturdy, well-fed goat for a sacrifice.
He examined it carefully, confirmed that it was healthy, and set off home with it over his shoulders.
Three hungry tricksters saw him.
Knowing that outright robbery might fail, they split up and arranged to meet him along the road in turn.
The first changed his clothes, approached the Brahmin, and asked in surprise:
“Why would someone so concerned with purity carry a dog on his shoulders?”
The Brahmin answered angrily:
“Can't you see? This is plainly a goat.”
The man did not argue further. He said only:
“Please don't be angry. You may think whatever you like.”
Farther along, the second man appeared.
Looking at the Brahmin's shoulders, he sighed:
“Even if that dead calf was once your pet, you shouldn't carry it like that. Contact with the dead brings impurity.”
Again the Brahmin objected:
“This is a live goat. How is it a dead calf?”
The second man did not insist either.
“Perhaps I was mistaken. Please carry on as you wish.”
Farther on, the third man approached.
He laughed and said:
“Why are you carrying a donkey on your shoulders? Put it down quickly, before more people see.”
This time, the Brahmin became frightened.
A dog, a dead calf, a donkey.
The three men had not said the same thing.
But all were certain that what he carried was not a goat.
Finally, he found an explanation:
Perhaps it was a spirit that kept changing shape.
He dropped the goat beside the road and fled in panic.
The three tricksters then reunited and took it away.
The story is often used to say:
Do not abandon facts you have verified with your own eyes merely because others repeatedly question them.
There is sense in that lesson.
The Brahmin had not casually assumed the goat was a goat. He had examined it, carried it, and directly felt its weight and body.
Yet three strangers, with only a few remarks, gradually undermined the credibility of experience right beside him.
But if we reduce the story to “Trust yourself, don't listen to others,” we go too far again.
People can of course be mistaken.
Several independent people identifying the same problem often give us precisely the reason to reexamine our own judgment.
If someone always believes:
I saw it with my own eyes, so I cannot be wrong.
They are no more reliable than the Brahmin, merely closed off in the opposite direction.
The question worth asking is not:
Should we trust ourselves or the majority?
It is:
**Are these voices actually independent pieces of evidence?**
On the surface, the Brahmin meets three strangers who do not know one another.
They appear in different places, dress differently, and show no connection.
Each encounter looks like a fresh verification.
The first man's “dog” can be dismissed as an accidental misidentification.
The second man's “dead calf” makes the Brahmin uneasy.
When the third says “donkey,” the outside world seems to have reached a consensus:
He alone still thinks he is carrying a goat.
But the three men have not made separate observations and independently reached their conclusions.
They planned together first, then deliberately appeared apart.
There are three people.
There is only one source of information.
Treating them as three independent pieces of evidence makes the Brahmin overestimate the weight of outside judgment.
This is what “Everyone says so” so easily conceals.
Ten people repeating a report does not necessarily mean ten people have checked it separately.
When many voices arise from the same rumor, reward, fear, or deliberately organized source, repetition produces scale without automatically increasing the factual basis.
The tricksters do not even say the same thing.
One says dog, one dead calf, one donkey.
Ordinary reasoning should make these conflicting accounts less credible.
If three people really see the same object independently, why do they reach three entirely different judgments?
But the Brahmin does not treat inconsistency as counterevidence.
He creates a larger explanation that contains all three conflicting claims:
It is a shape-shifting spirit.
The more contradictory the outside opinions become, the more plausible the spirit's “changeability” seems.
This step deserves attention.
We are not deceived only when evidence is insufficient.
Sometimes we actively invent an explanation that makes conflicting evidence support the same fear.
If the explanation is flexible enough, nothing can refute it.
Someone says dog, so it has turned into a dog.
Someone says donkey, so it has turned into a donkey again.
My own earlier sight of a goat presents no problem, because the spirit was originally disguised as a goat.
A story that explains everything often leaves no entrance through which facts can correct it.
The tricksters exploit more than the Brahmin's doubt about facts.
Each connects the question to his identity.
The first reminds him of purity.
The second emphasizes the consequences of touching something dead.
The third says others will laugh if they see him, and impurity will also need to be dealt with.
The question changes from “What animal is on my shoulders?” to:
“How could someone like you do such a thing?”
The Brahmin no longer worries only about misidentifying an animal.
He also fears that insisting on his judgment will make others see him as unfit for his religious role, ignorant of purity rules, or even unable to recognize what is before him.
When identity is threatened, we are more eager than usual to remove uncertainty.
By tying a factual question to respectability, purity, and shame, the tricksters keep him from stopping to examine the goat again. Instead, he hastens to discard what might prove him unworthy.
Each trickster leaves an apparently respectful way out:
“Perhaps I was mistaken.”
“Do as you think best.”
“Don't be angry. I'm only telling you what I see.”
They do not force the Brahmin to put the goat down.
The person who finally throws it away is indeed the Brahmin himself.
But performing an action oneself does not mean its conditions have not been carefully arranged by others.
The tricksters do not take away the form of his choice.
They change what each option means to him.
Continuing to carry the goat no longer means simply continuing his journey.
It has been rewritten as:
Risking impurity and humiliation to defend an abnormal judgment only he believes.
Putting the goat down becomes caution, self-protection, and restoration of identity.
With the options rearranged this way, the Brahmin still “decides for himself,” but inside a world designed by the tricksters.
This does not erase his own responsibility.
He began with direct evidence.
He could also stop, put the goat on the ground, watch how it moves and hear its call again, or wait for someone he actually knows to examine it with him.
The three strangers' words justify doubt, but need not immediately outweigh his recent observations.
The story works as a fable of strategy precisely because the tricksters accurately anticipate his response.
He is no puppet without choices.
He participates in completing the deception.
But acknowledging this does not mean the tricksters “merely said a few things” and therefore had no effect on his judgment.
Responsibility can lie in different places:
Those who design false evidence are responsible for creating the deception.
The person misled is responsible for checks they fail to perform.
The two need not cancel one another.
“Trust yourself” is not the whole solution either.
Some people reject every correction precisely because they trust themselves too much.
They can call every disagreement a conspiracy and every contrary fact a failure of others to understand, finally building another story that nothing can change.
What the Brahmin really lacks is not greater confidence.
It is an ability to recognize relationships among pieces of evidence:
Have these people each encountered the facts?
Are they really unconnected?
What motives do they have?
Are their accounts consistent?
Is there an inexpensive check I can still make in time?
Does my fear arise from the facts themselves, or from “What will people think of me?”
These questions cannot guarantee that we will never be deceived.
They merely keep “the majority” from automatically meaning “independent verification,” and “I saw it myself” from automatically becoming the final answer.
This Panchatantra story is not a modern epistemology class.
It sits within a framework of political strategy, illustrating how clever, coordinated tricksters obtain what they want from someone stronger than themselves.
The text may therefore not begin by condemning dishonesty in the manner of a modern moral tale.
What it admires is the strategy's effectiveness.
We need not hide that distance.
Precisely because the tricksters succeed, the story makes a common way of manufacturing “consensus” visible.
The three do not need the Brahmin to believe the same new fact.
They need only to stop him believing the original fact.
Once the goat is no longer securely a goat, fear will do the rest for them.
The Brahmin drops the goat because he thinks he is escaping a spirit.
In fact, he is escaping the world three voices have created in his mind.
In that world, his direct experience is no longer trustworthy, strangers' different claims jointly prove constant change, and maintaining his judgment threatens his identity.
The three tricksters then come together again.
Only then does it become visible that the apparently independent encounters were one plan from the start.
In reality, however, we rarely get to see those voices eventually enter the same room.
Faced with “Everyone says so,” we need neither resist at once nor comply at once.
First ask:
Do these people really know separately?
Three people can constitute three pieces of evidence only when they each encounter the facts and form their own judgments.
If they merely emerge from the same plan, however many more there are, they remain one voice in different clothes.

*Textual basis: “The Brahman's Goat” in Book III of Arthur W. Ryder's English translation of the Panchatantra. Ryder states that his translation follows Purnabhadra's Sanskrit recension of 1199, edited by Johannes Hertel, and that he supplied the story titles. The three tricksters call the goat a dog, a dead calf, and a donkey respectively, using religious purity and social respectability as pressure. The Brahmin finally interprets it as a shape-shifting spirit and abandons it. This essay retains the story's place within political strategy rather than presenting the modern moral “trust yourself” as its only conclusion.*
